sections.title: More Fallacies to Master
sections.content: Let's examine Slippery Slope, Appeal to Authority, and Circular Reasoning.
bullets: Slippery Slope — Assuming a small step leads to extreme outcomes
Appeal to Authority — Citing unqualified experts as proof
Circular Reasoning — The conclusion is assumed in the premise

sections.title: Why These Matter
sections.content: Slippery Slope exaggerates consequences. Appeal to Authority uses irrelevant expertise. Circular Reasoning assumes what it tries to prove.
bullets: Slippery Slope: 'Allow X, then Y will happen' — missing causal evidence
Appeal to Authority: 'This celebrity says it' — fame ≠ expertise
Circular Reasoning: 'It is true because it is true' — no external proof

sections.title: Circular Reasoning
sections.content: 'The Bible is true because it is the word of God. How do we know? Because the Bible says so.'
sections.explanation: The premise assumes the conclusion. No external evidence is provided.

sections.instruction: 'If we let students choose books, soon they won't read at all.' This is:
sections.feedback: Slippery Slope — assumes book choice leads to not reading, without evidence.

sections.q: An Appeal to Authority is fallacious when:
options: The authority is not an expert on this specific topic
sections.explain: Expertise in one field does not transfer. A physicist's opinion on economics is not automatically valid.

sections.instruction: Match each fallacy to its example.

pairs.right: Legalizing marijuana leads to societal collapse
My singer says this investment is safe
This law is just because it is fair

sections.sentence: A {0} {1} fallacy assumes one small change inevitably leads to extreme outcomes.
sections.feedback: Slippery Slope arguments need evidence for each causal step.

sections.statement: A "slippery slope" argument is always fallacious and should never be used in debate.
sections.feedback: Slippery slope is only fallacious when the causal chain is unsupported. A well-evidenced slippery slope can be a valid argument.

questions.argument: Dr. Smith, a Nobel physicist, says the economic stimulus will fail. The fallacy?
questions.feedback: Physics expertise does not qualify one as an economics authority.
